name: Battle of the Hydaspes
info: Alexander the Great's Macedonian army crossed the swollen Hydaspes in May 326 BCE and defeated the Pauravas under Porus on its bank in what is now Punjab, Pakistan; Alexander spared Porus and made him a satrap.

facts.place: The banks of the Hydaspes (Jhelum) river, in what is now the Punjab province of Pakistan
facts.sides: The Macedonian Empire under Alexander the Great, with the forces of Taxiles, king of Taxila; the Pauravas under Porus. Of the Macedonian army, an estimated 40,000 infantry and 5,000 cavalry crossed the river in time to fight; the Indian infantry outnumbered the Macedonian phalanx 5 to 1
facts.outcome: The Macedonians won and captured Porus. Large areas of Punjab were absorbed into the Macedonian Empire, and Alexander reinstated Porus as a satrap.

t: Alexander crossed the monsoon-swollen river about 27 km upstream of his camp, using feints and deception to keep Porus from learning where and when.

The Indian war elephants did heavy damage to the Macedonian foot, but they were driven back and trampled many of their own side, and the Macedonian cavalry and phalanx then closed on the Indian army from both sides.

Arrian gives Macedonian losses of 80 foot soldiers, ten horse archers, twenty Companions and 200 other horsemen, and Indian losses of 23,000; Diodorus has 12,000 Indians dead and over 9,000 captured, and J. F. C. Fuller thought his figure of 1,000 Macedonian dead more realistic.
dyk: Porus rode his tallest war elephant into the battle, against the usual custom of Indian kings of fighting from a chariot, and the animal carried no howdah because the king wore chain mail.
ev: Alexander defeats the last Achaemenid forces under Bessus and Spitamenes
Alexander fortifies Bactria with 10,000 men and invades India through the Khyber Pass
Alexander allies with Taxiles of Taxila against Porus and camps on the north bank of the Hydaspes
Alexander crosses the river upstream by night in a storm and routs a force under Porus' son
The Macedonian cavalry and phalanx defeat the Indian cavalry and elephants and Porus is captured
Alexander founds Nikaia and Boukephala and leaves Porus his lands
Alexander's army refuses to go further at the Hyphasis, and he marches south along the Indus

sections.background:
After defeating the last Achaemenid forces under Bessus and Spitamenes in 328 BCE, Alexander began a new campaign in 327 BCE to extend his empire towards India. He fortified Bactria with 10,000 men and entered India through the Khyber Pass. A smaller force under his own command took the northern route and the fortress of Aornos, a place of mythological significance to the Greeks because Herakles was said to have failed to occupy it. The Hindu clans of the Hindu Kush gave his army the toughest opposition it had faced, and he won although outnumbered, by between 3 to 1 and 5 to 1 depending on the source.

In early spring of the next year Alexander allied with Taxiles (local name Ambhi), king of Taxila, and they combined their forces against Taxiles' neighbour Porus the Elder, king of the Hydaspes. Porus had refused Alexander's order to surrender and was preparing for war. Alexander had to subdue him to keep marching east: a strong opponent left on his flank would endanger further campaigns, and he could not show weakness if he wanted to keep the loyalty of the Indian princes already subdued. Porus in turn had to defend his kingdom and chose a place well suited to checking the advance.
sections.forces:
The Macedonian army was much the larger. An estimated 40,000 infantry and 5,000 cavalry crossed the river in time to fight. The detachment that crossed with Alexander consisted, according to the 2nd century CE Greek historian Arrian, of 6,000 on foot and 5,000 on horseback, though it was probably larger. Craterus stayed in the camp with most of the army, and Meleager, Attalus and Gorgias commanded other forces. Alexander had Dahae horse archers, the armoured Companion cavalry and the heavy infantry phalanx with its long sarissas.

Porus drew up with cavalry on both flanks, chariots in front, and in the centre infantry with war elephants stationed every fifty feet before them to deter the Macedonian cavalry. The elephants were heavily armoured and carried howdahs with three archers and javelin men. Porus' soldiers wore bright clothes and steel helmets and carried axes, lances and maces. The Indian infantry outnumbered the phalanx by 5 to 1 but lacked armour and was at a disadvantage at close quarters against the sarissas. Alexander saw that the Indian line was strongest in the centre and planned to attack the flanks with his cavalry first, keeping the phalanx back until the Indian cavalry had been neutralised.
sections.course:
Alexander camped on the north bank of the Hydaspes, which was deep and fast enough that a direct crossing would probably doom the attackers. Porus shadowed Alexander's cavalry as it moved up and down the bank each night. Alexander used feints, detours and, it was reported, a look-alike in a mock royal tent to lull Porus. Alexander crossed about 27 km upstream, where a wooded island divided the river, on skin floats filled with hay and on boats cut in half. He first landed on the island by mistake. A storm that night drowned out the noise.

Porus sent his son with a small force of cavalry and chariots against the landing. Alexander's horse archers showered it with arrows, his heavy cavalry charged at once, and the chariots were stuck in the mud. The younger Porus died and his force was routed. The elder Porus left a detachment opposite Craterus and marched against Alexander. The Dahae harassed the Indian right and Alexander led the Companions against the left. The rest of the Indian cavalry came to help, Coenus attacked it from the rear, and it fled to the elephants.

The elephants advanced and caused heavy losses among the Macedonian foot, but the infantry resisted with javelins and axes, and the elephants were driven back and trampled many of their own side. The phalanx locked shields and advanced while the cavalry charged from the rear, and the Indian army broke. Craterus crossed and joined the pursuit. Alexander is said to have admired Porus' courage and sent several messengers before Meroes, a friend of Porus, persuaded the thirsty king to dismount and be taken to him.
sections.aftermath:
According to Arrian, Macedonian losses were 80 foot soldiers, ten horse archers, twenty Companions and 200 other horsemen. J. F. C. Fuller thought Diodorus' report of 1,000 killed more realistic. Indian losses were 23,000 according to Arrian and over 12,000 dead and over 9,000 captured according to Diodorus. Two sons of Porus, his relative and ally Spitakes and most of his chieftains were killed. Around 80 elephants were captured alive, and Alexander gained 70 more when reinforcements called by Porus arrived late and surrendered.

Asked how he wished to be treated, Porus replied "Treat me as a king would treat another king". Alexander let him keep his lands. He founded two cities, Nikaia at the site of the battle, named after the Greek word for victory, and Boukephala on the opposite bank, for his horse Bucephalus, who died during or after the battle.

Alexander then marched east towards the Nanda Empire but stopped at the Hyphasis (the Beas) in 326 BCE. His army, tired from nearly eight years of campaigning and worried about facing another very large Indian army, refused to go on. Historians do not call this a mutiny but a rise in military unrest. Alexander went south along the Indus instead, securing its banks as the borders of his empire, and left Porus in charge of the easternmost territory.
sections.sources:
The battle is known mainly through Greek historians, among them Arrian, who wrote in the 2nd century CE, and Diodorus. They differ on losses, and the totals for the Indian dead given by the two are close if Arrian counted prisoners in his figure. Fuller preferred Diodorus' Macedonian figure of 1,000 dead to Arrian's much smaller one.

Some details rest on report alone: the look-alike in the royal tent, and Alexander's growing admiration for Porus. Arrian's figure of 6,000 foot and 5,000 horse for the crossing force is thought probably too small. Peter Green judged that Porus' performance outclassed that of Memnon of Rhodes and of Spitamenes. Greek historians agree that Porus fought bravely to the end.
sections.legacy:
Alexander's crossing in the face of the Indian army, despite close watch by the Pauravas, has been called one of his masterpieces in combat. The battle is counted a very significant event in the Wars of Alexander, because it exposed the Indian subcontinent to Greek political and cultural influences that would affect Greeks and Indians for centuries. Large areas of Punjab were absorbed into the Macedonian Empire, with Porus as satrap.

The main reasons for Porus' defeat were Alexander's tactics and the Macedonians' discipline and technology. The Indian chariots were inferior to the Greek cavalry, the Indians had no well supported military infrastructure or standing army, and Porus mainly tried to counter his opponent's moves instead of taking the initiative. The Hydaspes was the hardest fought of Alexander's engagements in India, and in what was possibly his most costly engagement Porus became his most successful recorded opponent.

Under the later Maurya Empire the tactician Kautilya took the battle as a lesson and stressed military training before battle. The first Mauryan emperor, Chandragupta, kept a standing army, and the chariot corps played a marginal part in Mauryan military organisation.

summary: In May 326 BCE Alexander the Great crossed the monsoon-swollen Hydaspes in secret, defeated the Pauravas under Porus and captured him. Porus was kept as a ruler under Alexander, and the army turned back at the Hyphasis.

notes: The lead and the Background section give a garbled sentence: 'Whilst possessing a much larger army, at the battle, an estimated 40,000 infantry and 5,000 cavalry crossed the river in time to engage the enemy.' I used it only as the number that crossed in time.
'Alexander suffered heavy losses compared to his earlier victories' and 'possibly their most costly engagement' appear in the article; used once in legacy, hedged.
Arrian's Indian total 23,000 vs Diodorus' 12,000 dead and 9,000+ captured; the article's own remark that Arrian may have added prisoners is an inference, kept as the article's.
Crossing force: Arrian's 6,000 foot and 5,000 horse, 'probably larger'; not reconciled with the 40,000 and 5,000 figure.
Article says Bucephalus died 'during or after the battle'; kept as such. The article's claim that Alexander 'mistakenly landed on an island' is given as it stands.
The article calls the victory 'decisive' and Porus 'the most successful recorded opponent'; I left 'decisive' out of the text.
The article says Alexander 'founded' the cities; the date within 326 BCE is not given.
Left out: the poisoned rods on the elephants, the thrown spear at Taxiles (violent detail not needed), Greek political influence claim kept in general form, Spitakes detail kept.
The 'Sources' section is short because the article says little about the sources.
